instruction: How much urea should I save if I apply farmyard manure to my rice?
output: Apply 6 tonnes of farmyard manure per acre and save 16 kg of nitrogen (35 kg urea) from the recommended fertilizer dose. The FYM also improves soil structure, organic carbon, and micronutrient availability. PAU recommends applying organic manures alongside chemical fertilizers for higher yield and soil health. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much urea can I save with press mud or poultry manure on my rice?
output: Both press mud (6 tonnes per acre) and poultry manure (2.5 tonnes per acre) save 25 kg of nitrogen (55 kg urea) per acre - more savings than FYM. Press mud and poultry manure are more nutrient-dense than farmyard manure. Apply before transplanting along with the reduced urea dose. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much urea do I save with prali char on my rice?
output: Apply 2.0 tonnes of prali char (paddy straw biochar) per acre and save 16 kg of nitrogen (35 kg urea) per acre. Bonus: prali char also increases crop yield by 10 percent on top of the urea savings. This is the highest yield-boosting option among PAU's organic amendments and turns paddy straw waste into a productive input rather than burning. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much fertilizer does green manure save in rice?
output: Green manuring (dhaincha, cowpea, or sunnhemp incorporated 6-8 weeks old, one day before transplanting) saves 25 kg of nitrogen (55 kg urea) per acre. Summer moong residue incorporation saves 16 kg N (35 kg urea). The green manure also improves soil structure and supplies micronutrients. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I have coarse textured (sandy) soil. How do I manage rice fertility?
output: On coarse textured soils, apply organic manures (6 tonnes FYM, OR 2.5 tonnes poultry manure, OR 6 tonnes pressmud, OR 2.5 tonnes rice straw compost per acre) or green manure or summer moong residue IN ADDITION TO the recommended dose of nitrogen. The standard 'reduce urea by X kg' table doesn't apply on sandy soils because they leak nitrogen and need full fertilizer plus the organic boost. This also ameliorates micronutrient deficiencies common in sandy rice-wheat fields. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much chemical fertilizer should I apply to my rice?
output: Without a soil test, PAU recommends 42 kg N, 12 kg P2O5, and 12 kg K2O per acre for all rice varieties EXCEPT PR 132. For PR 132 (nitrogen-efficient variety), use only 31.5 kg N. Sources: 90 kg neem-coated urea per acre (67.5 kg for PR 132), 27 kg DAP or 75 kg single superphosphate, and 20 kg muriate of potash. Apply phosphorus and potash only if soil tests low. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How is the fertilizer dose for PR 132 rice different from other varieties?
output: PR 132 needs only 31.5 kg N per acre, 25 percent less than other varieties (42 kg). That translates to 67.5 kg neem-coated urea instead of 90 kg. Phosphorus (12 kg P2O5) and potassium (12 kg K2O) requirements stay the same. Higher nitrogen on PR 132 risks lodging without yield benefit. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When and how should I apply phosphorus to rice?
output: Apply the whole of phosphorus and potassium before puddling, based on soil test. If you missed pre-puddling, phosphorus can be top-dressed up to 21 days after transplanting. PAU also says skip phosphorus application to rice IF the recommended dose was applied to the preceding wheat crop - residual phosphorus carries over. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What if I use 27 kg DAP for rice phosphorus?
output: When 27 kg DAP per acre is used as the phosphorus source in deficient soil, reduce the urea dose by 10 kg per acre. DAP contains 18 percent nitrogen alongside phosphorus, so applying full urea on top would over-supply nitrogen and risk lodging. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How should I split nitrogen application across the rice growing season?
output: Apply nitrogen in three equal splits to all recommended rice varieties. First split: within 7 days of transplanting. Second split: at 21 days after transplanting. Third split: timed to the variety's growth (short-duration varieties get the third split earlier than long-duration varieties). Splits prevent nitrogen leaching loss in flooded paddy and match supply to crop demand. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I apply the first nitrogen split to my transplanted rice?
output: Apply the first nitrogen split within 7 days of transplanting. This jump-starts tillering during early establishment when nitrogen demand is high but the seedlings can take up only what is in their immediate root zone. Use one-third of the total recommended nitrogen for the variety. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I apply the second nitrogen split to rice?
output: Apply the second nitrogen split at 21 days after transplanting. This boosts active tillering, which directly determines yield through panicle number per square metre. Use one-third of the total recommended nitrogen for the variety. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Can I save fertilizer by applying organic manure to my rice?
output: Yes. PAU specifies these urea savings per acre with organic amendments: 6 tonnes FYM saves 35 kg urea (16 kg N), 6 tonnes pressmud saves 55 kg urea (25 kg N), 2.5 tonnes poultry manure saves 55 kg urea, 2.4 tonnes gobar gas slurry saves 35 kg urea, 2.0 tonnes prali char saves 35 kg urea AND boosts yield 10 percent, green manure saves 55 kg urea, summer moong residue saves 35 kg urea. Note: do NOT apply these savings on coarse-textured (sandy) soils where you should add organic plus full N. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I reduce sterility in my rice?
output: Apply foliar spray of 1.5 percent potassium nitrate (3 kg potassium nitrate dissolved in 200 litres of water per acre) at the boot stage of the rice crop. Sterility - empty grains - results from heat stress or nutrient imbalance during panicle initiation; the potassium nitrate spray strengthens the developing florets and improves grain set. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What boot stage spray helps rice grain filling?
output: Apply 1.5 percent potassium nitrate foliar spray (3 kg potassium nitrate in 200 litres of water per acre) at the boot stage to reduce sterility and improve grain set. The boot stage is when the panicle is fully formed inside the flag leaf sheath, just before emergence - the most heat-sensitive and nutrient-demanding period. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What organic options work alongside chemical fertilizer in rice for soil health?
output: PAU recommends combining chemical fertilizers with: farmyard manure, pressmud, poultry manure, gobar gas plant slurry, prali char (paddy straw biochar), green manure (dhaincha/cowpea/sunnhemp), or summer moong residue incorporation. Each option has documented urea savings (16-25 kg N saved per acre) and improves soil organic carbon over time. Bio-fertilizer like Azospirillum (root dip before transplanting) adds free nitrogen fixation. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I apply the third nitrogen split for PR 126 rice?
output: Apply the third nitrogen split for PR 126 (the short-duration variety) at 35 days after transplanting. This is earlier than other varieties because PR 126 matures in just 93 days, so the late-stage nitrogen demand peaks sooner. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I apply the third nitrogen split for medium-duration rice varieties?
output: For all varieties other than PR 126, apply the third nitrogen split at 42 days after transplanting. PR 126 (short-duration, 93 days) gets its third split earlier at 35 days. The 42-day timing matches the panicle initiation and stem elongation period when nitrogen demand peaks for medium-duration varieties. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Should I apply urea in standing water?
output: No - apply the second and third nitrogen splits when water is NOT standing in the field. Drain or let the field dry first, broadcast the urea, then irrigate on the third day of fertilizer application. Applying in standing water leads to ammonia volatilization losses and reduces nitrogen use efficiency. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I want to use fish pond sediments in my rice field. How do I adjust fertilizer?
output: If you apply 6 tonnes per acre of fish pond sediments before transplanting paddy, reduce the recommended fertilizer dose by 25 percent. Fish pond sediments are rich in nutrients accumulated from the pond ecosystem and supplement chemical fertilizer. The 25 percent reduction applies across nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I use PAU-LCC for need-based urea on my rice?
output: Apply basal dose of 25 kg urea per acre at puddling. Start matching colour of the first fully exposed leaf from the top with the LCC at 7-day intervals starting 14 days after transplanting. If 6 or more out of 10 leaves are LIGHTER than LCC shade 4, apply 25 kg urea per acre. If colour equals or is darker than LCC shade 4, apply NO urea. Discontinue LCC use after flowering initiation. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What basal urea dose should I apply at puddling for rice?
output: Apply 25 kg urea per acre as basal dose at puddling when using PAU-LCC for need-based nitrogen management. Subsequent urea applications are decided by leaf colour readings every 7 days after the 14th day of transplanting - apply 25 kg/acre only when 6+ of 10 leaves are lighter than LCC shade 4. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Does PAU-LCC work for all rice varieties?
output: Yes - need-based nitrogen management using LCC holds good for ALL prevalent rice varieties grown in ALL types of soils in Punjab. It is especially beneficial for optimum nitrogen use when fields are amended with organic manures (FYM, pressmud, prali char, green manure, etc.) where prediction of soil N supply is harder. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I correctly read PAU-LCC for rice?
output: Three rules from PAU: (1) Always match leaf colour under the shade of your body, not in direct sun. (2) Selected leaves should be free of insect-pest incidence. (3) The crop should not be under water stress and other nutrients (P, K, Zn) should be supplied per recommendations. Match the first fully exposed leaf from the top of 10 representative plants. If 6 or more are lighter than shade 4, apply 25 kg urea per acre. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I stop using LCC and stop applying urea on rice?
output: Discontinue LCC use AND stop applying urea after the initiation of flowering. By flowering, the rice has set its yield potential through tillering and panicle initiation; further urea would cause lodging without yield benefit and may delay maturity. The grain-filling stage uses internal nitrogen translocation. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Where can I buy PAU-LCC for rice?
output: PAU-LCC is available at the PAU Seed Shop at Gate No. 1, Ludhiana, AND through Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs) and Farm Advisory Service Centres in different districts of Punjab. The same chart is used for both rice and wheat with different shade thresholds. It is inexpensive and pays back many times in saved urea costs. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What does zinc deficiency look like in rice?
output: Zinc deficiency symptoms appear 2-3 weeks after transplanting. Lower leaves become rusty brown near the base and ultimately dry up. Seedlings with zinc deficiency remain stunted and tillerless. The symptoms are common in alkaline Punjab soils. Apply zinc sulphate immediately when symptoms appear or preventively at puddling if previous crops on the same field had shown deficiency. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I correct zinc deficiency in my rice?
output: Apply 25 kg of zinc sulphate heptahydrate (21 percent Zn) per acre, OR 16 kg of zinc sulphate monohydrate (33 percent Zn) per acre at puddling if previous crop showed deficiency. If symptoms appear in growing crop, apply this same quantity as soon as possible. For deteriorated soils where deficiency persists in patches, broadcast 10 kg zinc sulphate heptahydrate or 6.5 kg zinc sulphate monohydrate per acre mixed with equal dry soil on affected patches only. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I see lower leaves of my rice turning rusty brown near the base. What's wrong?
output: This is classic zinc deficiency in rice, common 2-3 weeks after transplanting on Punjab alkaline soils. Apply 25 kg zinc sulphate heptahydrate (21 percent Zn) or 16 kg zinc sulphate monohydrate (33 percent Zn) per acre as soon as possible. The seedlings will be stunted and tillerless if untreated, hurting yield severely. For preventive treatment in repeat-deficient fields, apply at puddling next season. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What if zinc deficiency keeps appearing in patches even after I applied zinc sulphate?
output: On highly deteriorated soils, zinc deficiency sometimes returns in patches despite the recommended pre-puddling application. Spot-treat affected patches: broadcast 10 kg zinc sulphate heptahydrate per acre OR 6.5 kg zinc sulphate monohydrate per acre, mixed with equal quantity of dry soil, only on the affected areas. This targets correction without over-applying to the whole field. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Is 21 percent or 33 percent zinc sulphate better for rice?
output: Both work at PAU-equivalent rates. For pre-puddling or growing-crop deficiency: 25 kg zinc sulphate heptahydrate (21 percent Zn) OR 16 kg zinc sulphate monohydrate (33 percent Zn) per acre. For patch correction: 10 kg heptahydrate OR 6.5 kg monohydrate. The 33 percent monohydrate is more concentrated, saves transport and storage, and has gained popularity. Both supply similar elemental zinc when applied at the equivalent rates. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What does iron deficiency look like in rice?
output: Iron deficiency in rice shows as chlorosis (yellowing) of the youngest leaf about three weeks after transplanting. It typically appears under water-scarce conditions when iron uptake is hampered. Plants die and often the crop fails completely if untreated. Start giving copious irrigations as soon as chlorosis appears - water restoration usually resolves the deficiency. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: My rice's youngest leaves are turning yellow at three weeks. What's wrong?
output: This pattern - chlorosis in the youngest leaf at about 3 weeks after transplanting - indicates iron deficiency, typically triggered by water scarcity. Start copious irrigations immediately as soon as chlorosis appears. If untreated, plants die and the crop can fail completely. Dhaincha green manure preceding rice also reduces iron deficiency risk. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I prevent iron deficiency in rice?
output: Iron deficiency in rice is triggered by water scarcity. Maintain adequate irrigation - especially during the first 3 weeks after transplanting. Dhaincha green manuring before rice also ameliorates iron deficiency by mobilizing soil iron. If chlorosis appears in youngest leaves at week 3, give copious irrigations immediately. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I treat iron deficiency in rice with foliar spray?
output: Apply 2 or 3 sprays of 1 percent ferrous sulphate solution at weekly intervals - that is 1 kg of ferrous sulphate dissolved in 100 litres of water per acre. Start as soon as you see chlorosis in the youngest leaves. Combine with copious irrigation to address the underlying water scarcity that triggered the deficiency. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How long should I keep water standing in my rice field after transplanting?
output: Keep water standing continuously for only TWO WEEKS after transplanting so seedlings get properly established. After that, apply irrigation two days after the ponded water has infiltrated into the soil. The depth of standing water should not exceed 10 cm. Continuous flooding wastes water without yield benefit. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How can I use a tensiometer to save irrigation water in rice?
output: Install a tensiometer at 15-20 cm soil depth. Irrigate when soil matric tension reaches 150 plus or minus 20 cm, OR when the water level in the tensiometer enters the yellow strip. This is precision irrigation timing - water is applied only when the soil actually needs it, saving significant water without yield reduction. Take care that the field does not develop cracks. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the maximum depth of standing water I should keep in my rice field?
output: The depth of standing water should not exceed 10 cm in transplanted rice. Deeper water wastes irrigation, reduces oxygen in the root zone, and can promote rotting of the lower stems. After the establishment period (first 2 weeks of continuous flooding), maintain shallow standing water with intermittent irrigation. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Should I drain my rice field before weeding?
output: Yes - drain away excess water before interculturing or weeding operations, then irrigate the field again after the operation. Working in standing water makes weeding harder and damages young rice tillers. Drain shortly before, do the work, then re-flood. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I stop irrigating rice before harvest?
output: Stop irrigation about a fortnight (15 days) before maturity. This allows the field to dry enough for combine harvesting and lets the wheat or other rabi crop be sown on schedule. Continued late irrigation delays harvest, makes combine operation impossible without rutting, and risks pushing wheat sowing past the optimum window. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I harvest my rice?
output: Harvest the rice crop when the ears are NEARLY ripened and straw has turned yellow. Do NOT delay until the crop is dead ripe - shattering of grains occurs and milling quality drops. The narrow window between nearly-ripe and dead-ripe is when both grain weight and quality are at peak. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What happens if I delay harvesting my rice past dead ripe stage?
output: Delayed harvest past dead ripe causes shattering of grains - mature grains fall to the ground and are lost. Milling quality of the grains is also affected: more breakage and lower head rice recovery. Harvest as soon as ears are nearly ripened and straw has turned yellow, even if other field operations compete for time. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Can I use a combine harvester for paddy?
output: Yes - combines are successfully used for harvesting paddy. Operate the combine at the proper speed for clean threshing without grain damage. Prefer combines fitted with a PAU Super SMS (Straw Management System) for chopping and even distribution of straw across the field. After SMS-equipped combine harvest, wheat can be directly sown with Happy Seeder without burning paddy straw. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the PAU Super SMS and why should I use it on my combine?
output: The PAU Super SMS (Straw Management System) is a combine attachment that chops paddy straw into small pieces and distributes them evenly across the field during harvest. After SMS-equipped combine harvest, the field is ready for direct wheat sowing with Happy Seeder - no straw burning required. This solves the air pollution crisis caused by paddy straw burning while saving labour and time before wheat sowing. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I sow wheat after rice without burning paddy straw?
output: Use a combine fitted with a PAU Super SMS (Straw Management System) to harvest paddy. The SMS chops straw and distributes it evenly across the field during harvest. Then directly sow wheat with a Happy Seeder, which cuts through the residue and seeds wheat in one pass. No burning needed. This is PAU's recommended approach for solving the paddy straw burning problem. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What other equipment can I use for harvesting paddy besides combine?
output: Tractor-drawn vertical conveyor reaper windrower can also be used for harvesting paddy. Multi-crop threshers can be used for threshing the harvested paddy. See Annexure V of the PAU Package of Practices for the full equipment list. Combines with PAU Super SMS remain the most efficient option for large fields. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I produce pure seed of my rice variety on my own farm?
output: Select a good plot of standing rice crop and rogue it thoroughly - remove all admixture plants and diseased plants. Harvest and thresh this plot separately from the main field. Dry the produce well and store separately in disinfested bins. This farm-saved pure seed maintains varietal identity and disease-free status for your next sowing. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is roguing and why do I do it for rice seed production?
output: Roguing is the process of inspecting your standing rice crop and physically removing any off-type plants (different variety mix-ins) and diseased plants before harvest. Walk through the plot multiple times during the season. Removing these undesirable plants ensures the seed you save next year is pure to the variety and free from seed-borne diseases. Combined with separate harvest, threshing, and storage, roguing maintains seed quality. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the maximum allowed moisture content for rice marketing?
output: As per specified norms, paddy moisture content should not exceed 17 percent at the time of marketing. Higher moisture risks rejection or price docking. Drier produce stores better and brings full price. Use sun drying or thresher fan to bring moisture down before taking to market. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What charges should I pay when marketing my rice?
output: As per the specified norms in Punjab, the farmer pays only unloading and cleaning charges on the produce delivered to the market. Other commission and handling charges are paid by the buyer. Get a J form from the commission agent as proof of sale. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the J form for rice marketing?
output: The J form is the official sale receipt issued by the commission agent (arhtia) when you sell paddy in a Punjab mandi. PAU advises farmers to always obtain the J form from the commission agent because it serves as proof of sale, supports MSP claims, and is needed for various government schemes and subsidy applications. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Why does PAU say excessive nitrogen at flowering causes yield loss?
output: Excessive nitrogen during flowering causes sterility - empty grains in the panicle - and consequently heavy reduction in yield. The lush canopy from over-fertilization also lodges and shades developing panicles. PAU's split application schedule (third split at 35-42 days, NO urea after flowering, LCC stops at flowering) is designed to prevent this damage. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.
